s-c1-1.s: There was a man called Ægir, or Hlér. He lived on the island now called Hlésey, and was deeply skilled in black magic. He made his way to Ásgard, but the Æsir knew of his journey beforehand. He was given a warm welcome, and yet many things were done by deceit, with illusions to deceive the eyes. In the evening, when it was time to drink, Odin had swords brought into the hall, so bright that light shone from them, and no other light was used while they sat drinking.

s-c1-2.s: Then the Æsir came in to their banquet, and the twelve Æsir who were appointed judges sat down in the high seats. These were their names: Thor, Njördr, Freyr, Týr, Heimdallr, Bragi, Vídarr, Váli, Ullr, Hœnir, Forseti, Loki; and likewise the Ásynjur: Frigg, Freyja, Gefjun, Idunn, Gerdr, Sigyn, Fulla, Nanna. Ægir thought it splendid to look around him in the hall. The wall panels were all hung with fine shields; there was heady mead too, and plenty of it was drunk. The man sitting next to Ægir was Bragi, and they drank and talked together. Bragi told Ægir of many things that had happened among the Æsir.

s-c2-1.s: He began the story at the point where three of the Æsir, Odin, Loki and Hœnir, left home and wandered over mountains and wastelands, where food was hard to find. When they came down into a certain valley they saw a herd of oxen, took one of them and set about cooking it. When they thought it must be cooked they broke up the fire, and it was not cooked. After a while they scattered the fire a second time, and still it was not cooked. They talked it over, asking one another what this could mean.

s-c2-2.s: Then they heard a voice in the oak above them: the one sitting there said that it was he who had taken the power from the fire. They looked up, and there sat an eagle, and no small one.

s-c2-3.s: Then the eagle said: "If you are willing to give me my fill of the ox, it will cook in the fire."

s-c2-4.s: They agreed to this. Then he let himself glide down from the tree, settled by the fire, and straight away took for himself the two hams of the ox and both shoulders.

s-c2-5.s: Then Loki grew angry, snatched up a great pole, swung it with all his strength and drove it at the eagle's body. The eagle lurched violently at the blow and flew up, and the pole stuck fast to the eagle's back, and Loki's hands to the other end of the pole. The eagle flew at such a height that Loki's feet knocked against stones, heaps of rock and trees down below, and he thought his arms would be torn from his shoulders. He cried out, begging the eagle desperately for peace; but the eagle said that Loki would never be set free unless he swore an oath to get Idunn to come out of Ásgard with her apples. Loki agreed, was set free at once and went back to his companions. Nothing more is told of their journey this time until they had come home.

s-c2-6.s: At the appointed time Loki lured Idunn out of Ásgard into a certain wood, saying that he had found some apples she would think very precious, and asked her to bring her own apples with her and compare them with these. Then the giant Thjazi came there in his eagle's plumage, seized Idunn and flew away with her, off to his home in Thrymheimr.

s-c3-1.s: But the Æsir were in great distress at Idunn's disappearance, and they quickly grew grey and old. Then the Æsir held a council, and each asked the others what had last been known of Idunn; and the last anyone had seen was that she had gone out of Ásgard with Loki. So Loki was seized and brought to the Thing, and threatened with death or torture. Once he was thoroughly frightened, he said that he would go after Idunn in Jötunheim, if Freyja would lend him the hawk's plumage that she owned.

s-c3-2.s: When he had the hawk's plumage he flew north into Jötunheim, and came one day to the home of the giant Thjazi. Thjazi had rowed out to sea, and Idunn was at home alone. Loki turned her into a nut, gripped her in his claws and flew as fast as he could.

When Thjazi came home and found Idunn gone, he took his eagle's plumage and flew after Loki, his wings making a mighty rushing sound as he flew. When the Æsir saw the hawk flying with the nut, and where the eagle was flying, they went out below Ásgard and carried loads of wood shavings there. As soon as the hawk flew into the stronghold he swooped down close by the wall, and then the Æsir set fire to the shavings. The eagle could not stop himself when he missed the hawk: his feathers caught fire, and at once his flight was over. The Æsir were close at hand and killed the giant Thjazi inside the Gate of the Æsir, and that killing is very famous.

s-c3-3.s: Now Skadi, the daughter of the giant Thjazi, took helmet and mail-coat and all the weapons of war and went to Ásgard to avenge her father. But the Æsir offered her a settlement and compensation. The first term was that she should choose herself a husband from among the Æsir, and choose him by his feet alone, seeing no more of him.

s-c3-4.s: Then she saw one man's feet, which were very beautiful, and said: "I choose this one: there can be little that is ugly about Baldr."

s-c3-5.s: But it was Njördr of Nóatún.

s-c3-6.s: She also had this term in her settlement: that the Æsir must do something she thought they would not be able to do, and make her laugh. Then Loki did this: he tied a cord to the beard of a goat and the other end around his own genitals, and each gave way in turn, and both of them screeched loudly. Then Loki let himself fall onto Skadi's knee, and she laughed. With that the Æsir's settlement with her was made.

s-c4-1.s: It is said that Odin did this to compensate Skadi: he took Thjazi's eyes, threw them up into the sky and made two stars of them.

s-c4-2.s: Then Ægir said: "It seems to me that Thjazi was a mighty man. What family did he come from?"

s-c4-3.s: Bragi answered: "His father was called Ölvaldi, and if I tell you about him you will think it a marvel. He was very rich in gold; and when he died and his sons came to divide the inheritance, they settled on this measure for the gold they were dividing: each should take as much as his mouth would hold, and all of them the same number of mouthfuls. One of them was Thjazi, the second Idi, the third Gangr. And now we have it as a metaphor among us to call gold the mouth-count of these giants; but we conceal it in secret language or in poetry by calling it the Speech, or Word, or Talk, of these giants."

s-c4-4.s: Then Ægir said: "I think that is well concealed in secret language."

s-c5-1.s: And Ægir spoke again: "Where did this art that you call poetry have its beginnings?"

s-c5-2.s: Bragi answered: "This is how it began. The gods had a dispute with the people called the Vanir, and they arranged a peace meeting between them and made peace in this way: both sides went to a vat and spat into it. Then, when they parted, the gods took that token of peace and would not let it be lost, but made a man out of it. This man is called Kvasir, and he was so wise that no one could ask him a question about anything that he could not answer.

s-c5-3.s: He travelled far and wide over the earth teaching people; and when he came by invitation to the home of certain dwarves, Fjalar and Galarr, they called him aside for a private talk and killed him, letting his blood run into two vats and a cauldron. The cauldron is called Ódrerir, and the vats Són and Bodn. They mixed honey with the blood, and the result was the mead that makes whoever drinks it a poet or a scholar. The dwarves told the Æsir that Kvasir had choked on his own cleverness, since there was no one there wise enough to question his wisdom.

s-c5-4.s: "Then these dwarves invited the giant called Gillingr to visit them, and his wife with him. Next the dwarves invited Gillingr to row out to sea with them; but when they had gone out from the land, the dwarves rowed into the breakers and capsized the boat. Gillingr could not swim, and he died; but the dwarves righted their boat and rowed to land. They told his wife of this accident, and she took it badly and wept loudly. Then Fjalar asked her whether it would ease her heart to look out to sea at the place where he had died, and she wanted to. Then he spoke quietly to his brother Galarr, telling him to climb up above the doorway as she went out and drop a millstone on her head, saying that he was growing tired of her weeping; and so he did.

s-c5-5.s: "Now when the giant Suttungr, Gillingr's son, heard of this, he went there, seized the dwarves, carried them out to sea and set them on a reef that was covered at high tide. They begged Suttungr to spare their lives, and as the price of a settlement offered him the precious mead in compensation for his father's death. And on those terms they were reconciled. Suttungr carried the mead home and hid it in the place called Hnitbjörg, setting his daughter Gunnlöd there to guard it. Because of this we call poetry Kvasir's Blood, or Dwarves' Drink, or Fill, or any kind of liquid of Ódrerir, or of Bodn, or of Són, or Ferry-Boat of Dwarves, since this mead brought them ransom for their lives from the reef, or Suttungamjödr, or Liquor of Hnitbjörg."

s-c5-6.s: Then Ægir said: "These seem to me obscure expressions, to call poetry by these names. But how did you Æsir get hold of Suttungamjödr?"

s-c6-1.s: Bragi answered: "The story goes like this. Odin left home and came to a place where nine slaves were mowing hay. He asked whether they would like him to sharpen their scythes, and they said yes. Then he took a whetstone from his belt and sharpened the scythes. It seemed to them that the scythes cut far better, and they asked to buy the whetstone. But he set such a value on it that whoever wanted to buy it must pay a considerable price. All the same, they all said they would agree, and asked him to sell it to them. He threw the whetstone up into the air; and since they all wanted to get their hands on it, they became so tangled up with one another that each struck his scythe against another's neck.

s-c6-2.s: "Odin sought a night's lodging with the giant called Baugi, Suttungr's brother. Baugi complained about the state of his farm, saying that his nine slaves had killed one another, and declared that he had no hope of finding workmen. Odin gave his name to Baugi as Bölverkr. He offered to do nine men's work for Baugi, and asked as his wages one drink of Suttungamjödr. Baugi said that he had no say at all over the mead, and that Suttungr was determined to keep it to himself, but he promised to go with Bölverkr and see whether they could get the mead.

s-c6-3.s: During the summer Bölverkr did nine men's work for Baugi, and when winter came he asked Baugi for his pay. Then they both set out for Suttungr's home. Baugi told his brother Suttungr of his bargain with Bölverkr, but Suttungr flatly refused them a single drop of the mead. Then Bölverkr suggested to Baugi that they should try some tricks, to see whether they could find a way to get at the mead, and Baugi readily agreed. Bölverkr then brought out the auger called Rati, and said that Baugi must bore into the rock, if the auger would cut. He did so. At last Baugi said that the rock was bored through, but Bölverkr blew into the auger hole, and the chips flew back at him. Then he realised that Baugi meant to deceive him, and told him to bore right through the rock. Baugi bored again; and when Bölverkr blew a second time, the chips were blown inwards. Then Bölverkr turned himself into a serpent and crawled into the auger hole, and Baugi stabbed after him with the auger and missed him.

s-c6-4.s: Bölverkr went on to where Gunnlöd was, and lay with her for three nights; and then she let him drink three draughts of the mead. In the first draught he drank every drop out of Ódrerir, in the second he emptied Bodn, and in the third Són; and then he had all the mead. Then he turned himself into an eagle and flew as hard as he could; but when Suttungr saw the eagle's flight, he too took the shape of an eagle and flew after him.

s-c6-5.s: When the Æsir saw Odin flying, they at once set their vats out in the courtyard; and when Odin came into Ásgard he spat the mead up into the vats. But he came so close to being caught by Suttungr that he sent some of the mead out backwards, and no notice was taken of that: anyone who wanted it could have it, and we call it the bad poets' share. But Odin gave Suttungamjödr to the Æsir and to those people who have the skill to compose. That is why we call poetry Odin's Booty and Find, and his Drink and Gift, and the Drink of the Æsir."

s-c7-1.s: Then Ægir said: "In how many ways are the terms of poetry varied, and how many essential elements are there in the poet's art?"

s-c7-2.s: Then Bragi answered: "There are two elements into which all poetry is divided."

s-c7-3.s: Ægir asked: "Which two?" Bragi said: "Metaphor and metre."

s-c7-5.s: "What kind of metaphor is used in the poets' writing?" "There are three types of poetic metaphor."

s-c7-8.s: "Which?" "These: [first], calling everything by its name; the second type is the one called 'substitution'; the third type of metaphor is the one called 'periphrasis', and this type is used in the following way. Suppose I take Odin, or Thor, or Týr, or any of the Æsir or Elves; and to whichever of them I mention, I add the name of something belonging to another of the Æsir, or I mention certain of his deeds. Then that other one becomes the owner of the name, and not the one whose name was applied to him. So when we speak of Victory-Týr, or Týr of the Hanged, or Týr of Cargoes, that becomes a name of Odin; and we call these periphrastic names. So also with the title Týr of the Chariot.

s-c8-1.s: "But now one thing must be said to young poets, to those who long to master the craft of poetry and to enlarge their stock of figures with traditional metaphors, or to those who want to gain the ability to understand what is said in veiled language: let such a person, then, interpret this book for his instruction and pleasure. Yet these traditions are not to be so forgotten or discredited as to remove from poetry the ancient metaphors with which the chief poets have been pleased to content themselves. Nor, on the other hand, should Christian people believe in heathen gods, or in the truth of these tales in any other way than exactly as it is found here at the beginning of the book.

s-c12-1.s: "How should one periphrase Baldr? By calling him Son of Odin and Frigg, Husband of Nanna, Father of Forseti, Possessor of Hringhorni and Draupnir, Adversary of Hödr, Companion of Hel, God of Tears. Úlfr Uggason, following the story of Baldr, composed a long passage in the Húsdrápa; and examples have been recorded earlier showing that Baldr is referred to in this way.

s-c15-1.s: "How should one periphrase Heimdallr? By calling him Son of Nine Mothers, or Watchman of the Gods, as has already been written; or White God, Foe of Loki, Seeker of Freyja's Necklace. A sword is called Heimdallr's Head, for it is said that he was pierced by a man's head. The story is told in Heimdalar-galdr; and ever since a head has been called Heimdallr's Measure, and a sword is called Man's Measure. Heimdallr is the Possessor of Gulltoppr; he is also Frequenter of Vágasker and Singasteinn, where he fought with Loki for the necklace Brísinga-men. He is also called Vindlér. Úlfr Uggason composed a long passage in the Húsdrápa on that legend, and it is recorded there that they were in the form of seals. Heimdallr is also a son of Odin.

s-c16-1.s: "How should one periphrase Týr? By calling him the One-handed God, and Fosterer of the Wolf, God of Battles, Son of Odin.

s-c24-1.s: "Now an account shall be given of where those metaphors come from which have just been recorded, and which have not been explained before: such as the one Bragi gave to Ægir, telling how Thor had gone into the east to kill trolls, and Odin rode Sleipnir into Jötunheim and visited the giant called Hrungnir. Hrungnir asked what sort of man this was in the golden helmet, who rode through air and water, and said that the stranger had a wonderfully good horse. Odin said he would wager his head that there was no horse in Jötunheim that would prove as good. Hrungnir answered that it was a good horse, but declared that he had a horse with a much better stride, called Gold-Mane. Hrungnir had grown angry; he leapt onto his horse and galloped after him, meaning to pay him back for his boasting. Odin galloped so hard that he was on the top of the next hill first; but Hrungnir was so filled with a giant's fury that he noticed nothing until he had come in through the gates of Ásgard.

s-c24-2.s: When he came to the door of the hall, the Æsir invited him to drink. He went inside and called for drink to be brought to him, and the flagons that Thor usually drank from were brought in; Hrungnir gulped from each in turn. But once he had become drunk there was no shortage of big words: he boasted that he would lift up Valhall and carry it to Jötunheim, sink Ásgard and kill all the gods, except that he would take Freyja and Sif home with him. Freyja alone dared to pour for him, and he swore that he would drink all the ale of the Æsir.

s-c24-3.s: But when the Æsir grew tired of his overbearing insolence, they called on the name of Thor.

"At once Thor came into the hall, brandishing his hammer. He was very angry, and asked who had decided that these dogs of giants should be allowed to drink there, who had granted Hrungnir safe-conduct to be in Valhall, and why Freyja should pour for him as at a feast of the Æsir.

s-c24-4.s: Then Hrungnir answered, giving Thor no friendly look, and said that Odin had invited him to drink and that he was under his safe-conduct. Thor declared that Hrungnir would regret that invitation before he got away.

s-c24-5.s: Hrungnir answered that Ása-Thor would win little glory by killing him, unarmed as he was: it would be a greater test of his courage if he dared to fight Hrungnir on the border at Grjótúnagard. 'And it was very foolish of me,' he said, 'to leave my shield and whetstone behind at home; if I had my weapons here, we would try single combat. But as things stand, I declare you a coward if you kill me, an unarmed man.'

s-c24-6.s: Thor was by no means anxious to avoid the fight when challenged to the field, for no one had ever offered him single combat before.

"Then Hrungnir went on his way, and galloped hard until he came to Jötunheim. The news of his journey spread among the giants, and word got about that a meeting had been arranged between him and Thor. The giants felt that they had a great deal at stake in who won the victory, since they expected the worst from Thor if Hrungnir was killed, he being the strongest of them all.

s-c24-7.s: Then the giants made a man of clay at Grjótúnagard: he was nine miles high and three broad under the armpits. But they could find no heart big enough to fit him until they took one from a mare. Even that did not hold steady inside him when Thor came.

s-c24-8.s: Hrungnir had the heart that is famous: of hard stone, and pointed with three corners, like the written character made since then which is called Hrungnir's Heart. His head was also of stone; his shield was stone too, wide and thick, and he held the shield in front of him as he stood at Grjótúnagard and waited for Thor. He also had a whetstone for a weapon, and brandished it over his shoulders, and he was not a pretty sight. On one side of him stood the clay giant, who was called Mökkurkálfi: he was terribly afraid, and it is said that he wet himself when he saw Thor.

s-c24-9.s: "Thor went to the meeting place, and Thjálfi with him.

s-c24-10.s: Then Thjálfi ran forward to where Hrungnir stood and said to him: 'You are standing carelessly, giant, with your shield in front of you: Thor has seen you, and he is coming here down under the earth, and will come at you from below.'

s-c24-11.s: Then Hrungnir pushed the shield under his feet and stood on it, gripping the whetstone with both hands. Very soon he saw lightning and heard great claps of thunder; then he saw Thor in his godlike anger, who came on furiously, swung the hammer and threw it at Hrungnir from a long way off. Hrungnir lifted the whetstone in both hands and threw it against him. It struck the hammer in flight and the whetstone broke apart: one part fell to the ground, and from it come all the flint rocks; the other smashed into Thor's head, so that he fell forward to the ground. But the hammer Mjöllnir struck Hrungnir in the middle of the head and smashed his skull into small crumbs, and he fell forward over Thor, so that his foot lay across Thor's neck. Thjálfi attacked Mökkurkálfi, and he fell with little glory.

s-c24-12.s: Then Thjálfi went over to Thor and tried to lift Hrungnir's foot off him, but did not have the strength. At once all the Æsir came up, when they learned that Thor had fallen, and tried to lift the foot off him, and could do nothing.

s-c24-13.s: Then Magni came up, the son of Thor and Járnsaxa. He was three nights old at the time. He threw Hrungnir's foot off Thor and said: 'See what a pity it is, father, that I came so late: I think I would have struck this giant dead with my fist if I had met him.'

s-c24-14.s: Thor got up and welcomed his son, saying that he would surely grow to be great. 'And I will give you,' he said, 'the horse Gullfaxi, which Hrungnir owned.'

s-c24-15.s: Then Odin spoke and said that Thor did wrong to give that good horse to the son of a giantess, and not to his father.

s-c25-1.s: "Thor went home to Thrúdvangar, and the whetstone stayed stuck in his head. Then the wise woman called Gróa came, the wife of Aurvandill the Valiant. She sang her spells over Thor until the whetstone began to come loose. When Thor noticed that, and thought there was hope that the whetstone might be removed, he wanted to reward Gróa for her healing and make her glad, and told her this news: that he had waded from the north over Icy Stream and had carried Aurvandill in a basket on his back, from the north out of Jötunheim. And as proof he added that one of Aurvandill's toes had stuck out of the basket and frozen, so Thor broke it off and threw it up into the sky, and made from it the star called Aurvandill's Toe. Thor said that it would not be long before Aurvandill came home. But Gróa was so overjoyed that she forgot her spells, and the whetstone came no looser, and it is still in Thor's head. That is why it is forbidden to throw a whetstone across the floor, for then the whetstone in Thor's head is stirred. Thjódólfr of Hvin has composed a poem on this story in the Haustlöng. s-c26-1.s: Then Ægir said: "Hrungnir seems to me to have been very mighty. Did Thor do even braver deeds when he had dealings with the trolls?" And Bragi answered: "The story of how Thor went to Geirrödargardar deserves to be told at length. At that time he did not have the hammer Mjöllnir with him, nor his Girdle of Might, nor the iron gauntlets, and that was the fault of Loki, who went with him. For once, when Loki was flying for amusement in Frigg's hawk-plumage, it happened that out of curiosity he flew into Geirrödr's court. There he saw a great hall, and he alighted and looked in through the window. Geirrödr looked up and saw him, and ordered the bird to be caught and brought to him. But the man who was sent could hardly get to the top of the wall, it was so high. Loki enjoyed seeing the man struggle so hard to reach him, and he decided not to fly away until the man had finished the dangerous climb. When the man was almost upon him, he spread his wings to fly and pushed off hard, but now his feet were stuck fast.

So Loki was caught and brought before the giant Geirrödr. When Geirrödr saw his eyes, he suspected that this might be a man, and told him to answer; but Loki was silent. Then Geirrödr shut Loki in a chest and starved him there for three months. When Geirrödr took him out and ordered him to speak, Loki said who he was; and to ransom his life he swore oaths to Geirrödr that he would get Thor to come to Geirrödr's dwelling with neither his hammer nor his Girdle of Might.

s-c26-2.s: "Thor came to spend the night with the giantess called Grídr, the mother of Vídarr the Silent. She told Thor the truth about Geirrödr: that he was a cunning giant and hard to deal with. She lent him the Girdle of Might and the iron gloves that she owned, and also her staff, which was called Grídarvölr.

s-c26-3.s: Then Thor went on to the river called Vimur, the greatest of all rivers. There he fastened the Girdle of Might around him and braced himself firmly against the current with Grídarvölr, while Loki held on behind by the Girdle of Might. When Thor reached the middle of the stream, the river rose so much that it broke high on his shoulders. Then Thor sang this:

l: for I want to wade through you
then my divine strength will rise in me

s-c26-5.s: "Then Thor saw Gjálp, Geirrödr's daughter, standing in a ravine astride the river, with one leg on each side, and she was causing the flood.

s-c26-6.s: Then Thor snatched a great stone out of the river and threw it at her, saying: 'A river should be dammed at its source.'

s-c26-7.s: And he did not miss what he threw at. At that moment he reached the bank, caught hold of a clump of rowan and so climbed out of the river; and that is the origin of the saying that the rowan is Thor's rescue.

s-c26-8.s: "When Thor came to Geirrödr, he and his companion were first shown into the goat-shed as their lodging. There was one chair there to sit on, and Thor sat on it. Then he noticed that the chair was moving under him, up towards the roof. He thrust Grídarvölr up against the rafters and pushed down hard on the chair. There was a great crash, followed by screaming. Under the chair had been Geirrödr's daughters, Gjálp and Greip, and he had broken both their backs.

s-c26-9.s: Then Geirrödr had Thor called into the hall to play games. There were great fires along the whole length of the hall. When Thor came up opposite Geirrödr, Geirrödr picked up a glowing bar of iron with the tongs and threw it at Thor. Thor caught it with his iron gloves and raised the bar in the air, but Geirrödr leapt behind an iron pillar to save himself. Thor lifted the bar and threw it, and it went through the pillar and through Geirrödr and through the wall, and so on outside into the earth.

s-c39-1.s: "How should man be periphrased? By his works, by what he gives or receives or does. He may also be periphrased in terms of his property, the things he owns, and, if he is generous, of his generosity; likewise in terms of the families he is descended from, as well as those that are descended from him. How is he to be periphrased in terms of these things? By calling him the accomplisher or performer of his journeys or his conduct, of his battles or sea voyages or hunts or weapons or ships. And because he is a tester of weapons and a winner of battles (the words for 'winner' and 'wood' being the same, as are those for 'tester' and 'rowan'), poets have, from these phrases, called man Ash or Maple, Grove, or other masculine tree-names, and periphrased him in such expressions in terms of battles or ships or possessions. It is also correct to periphrase man with all the names of the Æsir; also with giant-terms, and this is mostly for mockery or slander. Periphrasis with the names of elves is thought favourable.

"Woman should be periphrased with reference to all women's clothing, gold and jewels, ale or wine or any other drink, or to what she serves or gives; likewise with reference to ale-vessels, and to all the things that it is fitting for her to do or to give.

s-c39-2.s: It is correct to periphrase her like this: by calling her giver or user of what she shares in. But the words for 'giver' and 'user' are also names of trees; so woman is called in metaphorical speech by all feminine tree-names. Woman is periphrased with reference to jewels or agates for this reason: in heathen times what was called a 'stone-necklace', which they wore around the neck, was part of a woman's dress; now it is used figuratively, so that woman is periphrased with stones and all names of stones. Woman is also metaphorically called by the names of the Ásynjur or the Valkyries or Norns or women of supernatural kind. It is also correct to periphrase woman in terms of all her conduct or property or family.

s-c40-1.s: "How should gold be periphrased? By calling it Ægir's Fire, and Needles of Glasir, Hair of Sif, Headband of Fulla, Freyja's Tears, Talk and Voice and Word of Giants, Draupnir's Drop and Rain or Shower of Draupnir, or of Freyja's Eyes, Otter's Ransom, Forced Payment of the Æsir, Seed of Fýris-Plain, Cairn-Roof of Hölgi, Fire of all Waters and of the Hand, Stone and Reef or Gleam of the Hand.

s-c41-1.s: Why is gold called Ægir's Fire? This story is to the same effect as the one we told before: Ægir went to a feast in Ásgard, and when he was ready to go home he invited Odin and all the Æsir to visit him in three months' time. First came Odin and Njördr, Freyr, Týr, Bragi, Vídarr, Loki; likewise the Ásynjur: Frigg, Freyja, Gefjun, Skadi, Idunn, Sif. Thor was not there, as he had gone into the eastern lands to kill trolls. When the gods had sat down in their places, Ægir at once had bright gold brought in onto the floor of the hall, and the gold gave out light and lit up the hall like fire; it was used there for light at his banquet, just as in Valhall swords were used in place of fire. Then Loki traded sharp words with all the gods, and killed one of Ægir's slaves, the one called Five-Finger; another of his slaves was called Fire-Kindler. Rán is the name of Ægir's wife, and they have nine daughters, as we have written before. At this feast everything served itself, both food and ale, and all the utensils the feast needed. Then the Æsir discovered that Rán had the net in which she used to catch all men who go to sea.

s-c41-2.s: Now this story shows why gold is called Fire or Light or Brightness of Ægir, of Rán, or of Ægir's daughters; and such use is now made of these metaphors that gold is called Fire of the Sea, and of all names of the sea, just as Ægir or Rán had names associated with the sea. So gold is now called Fire of Waters or of Rivers, and of all river names.

"But these names have gone the same way as other figures: the later poets have composed after the examples of the old poets, the very examples that stood in their poems, but these were later expanded into such forms as seemed to later poets to be like what was written before: as a lake is to the sea, or the river to the lake, or the brook to the river. So all these are called new figures, when terms are expanded to greater length than what was recorded before; and all this seems well and good, so far as it agrees with likelihood and nature. As Bragi the poet sang:

l: I was given by the Battler
the fire of the Brook of Sea-Fish:
He gave it to me, with mercy,
for the Drink of the Mountain-Giant.

s-c43-1.s: "Why is gold called Sif's Hair? Loki Laufeyarson, out of mischief, cut off all Sif's hair. When Thor found out, he seized Loki and would have broken every bone in his body, had he not sworn to get the Black Elves to make Sif hair of gold that would grow like other hair. After that, Loki went to the dwarves called Ívaldi's Sons, and they made the hair, and Skídbladnir too, and the spear which became Odin's and was called Gungnir.

s-c43-2.s: Then Loki wagered his head with the dwarf called Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri could not make three other precious things as good as these. When they came to the smithy, Sindri laid a pigskin in the hearth and told Brokkr to blow, and did not stop work until he took out of the hearth what he had laid in it. But as soon as he went out of the smithy, while the other dwarf was blowing, a fly settled on his hand and stung him; yet he kept blowing as before, until the smith took the work out of the hearth, and it was a boar with a mane and bristles of gold. Next he laid gold in the hearth and told Brokkr to blow and not to stop blowing until he came back. He went out; but again the fly came and settled on Brokkr's neck, and bit half as hard again as before; yet he kept blowing until the smith took from the hearth the gold ring called Draupnir. Then Sindri laid iron in the hearth and told him to blow, saying that it would be spoiled if the blowing failed. At once the fly settled between Brokkr's eyes and stung his eyelid, and when the blood ran into his eyes so that he could not see, he snatched at it with his hand as quickly as he could, while the bellows went flat, and swept the fly off him. Then the smith came in and said that everything in the hearth had come close to being spoiled. Then he took a hammer from the forge, put all the precious works into the hands of his brother Brokkr, and told him to take them to Ásgard and claim the wager.

s-c43-3.s: "Now when he and Loki brought forward the precious gifts, the Æsir sat down in the seats of judgement, and the verdict given by Odin, Thor and Freyr was to stand. Then Loki gave Odin the spear Gungnir, Thor the hair that Sif was to have, and Freyr Skídbladnir, and explained the virtues of all these things: the spear would never stop in its thrust; the hair would grow to the flesh as soon as it was placed on Sif's head; and Skídbladnir would have a fair wind as soon as the sail was raised, wherever it was bound, but could be folded up like a napkin and kept in Freyr's pouch if he wished.

s-c43-4.s: Then Brokkr brought forward his gifts. He gave Odin the ring, saying that eight rings of the same weight would drop from it every ninth night. To Freyr he gave the boar, saying that it could run through air and water better than any horse, and that it could never grow so dark with night or with the gloom of the Murky Regions that there would not be enough light wherever it went, such was the glow from its mane and bristles. Then he gave the hammer to Thor, and said that Thor could strike as hard as he liked, whatever was in front of him, and the hammer would not fail; if he threw it at anything it would never miss, and never fly so far that it would not return to his hand; and if he wished he could keep it inside his shirt, it was so small. But the hammer did have one flaw: the handle was rather short.

s-c43-5.s: "This was their decision: that the hammer was the best of all the precious works, and that it was the greatest defence against the frost giants; and they ruled that the dwarf had won his wager.

s-c43-6.s: Then Loki offered to redeem his head, but the dwarf said there was no chance of that. 'Take me, then,' said Loki; but when Brokkr tried to lay hands on him, he was a long way off.

s-c43-7.s: Loki had with him the shoes with which he ran through the air and over water.

s-c43-8.s: Then the dwarf asked Thor to catch him, and Thor did so. The dwarf was about to cut off his head, but Loki said that he could have the head, but not the neck. So the dwarf took a thong and a knife, and tried to bore a hole in Loki's lips and stitch his mouth together, but the knife would not cut. Then Brokkr said that it would be better if his brother's awl were there; and as soon as he named it, the awl was there, and it pierced the lips. He stitched the lips together, and Loki ripped the thong out through the edges. The thong with which Loki's mouth was sewn together is called Vartari.

s-c44-1.s: "One can hear how gold is metaphorically called Fulla's Headband in this verse composed by Eyvindr Skald-Despoiler:

l: for poets all Hakon's life long.

s-c44-3.s: "Gold is called Freyja's Tears, as was said before. As Skúli Thorsteinsson sang:

l: all the more that morning when we
killed our enemies; we were there.
swollen with the gold of the Serpent's lair.

s-c44-7.s: And here Einarr has further periphrased Freyja by calling her Mother of Hnoss, or Wife of Ódr, as follows:

l: The shield, the tempest's strong roof-ice,
so the King spends his age.
I own, wound with gold, a jewel
most beautiful; to the shield's rim
Freyr's Niece carries on the gem
gave me the fostering of Fródi's seed-gold.

s-c44-11.s: It is also recorded here that Freyja may be periphrased by calling her Sister of Freyr.

l: A very fine defence of songs
the golden gem-child of Njördr's Daughter.

s-c44-13.s: Here she is called Daughter of Njördr.

l: of the Vana-Bride, my fine axe;
the valiant Ruler of the sword-meeting
led Gefn's girl to the poet's bed,
set with the gold-work of the sea-flame.

s-c44-15.s: Here she is called Gefn and Bride of the Vanir. It is proper to join 'tears' with all the names of Freyja, and to call gold by such terms; and these periphrases have been varied in many ways, so that gold is called Hail, or Rain, or Snow-Storm, or Drops, or Showers, or Waterfalls, of Freyja's Eyes, or Cheeks, or Brows, or Eyelids.

s-c45-1.s: "Here one can hear that gold is called Word, or Voice, of Giants, as we have said before. As Bragi the poet sang:

l: Then I had the third friend,
in the Voice of the Botched-Knob's Áli,
but the best of all to me.

s-c45-3.s: He called a rock Botched Knob, and a giant Áli of Rock, and gold Voice of the Giant.

s-c46-1.s: "Why is gold called Otter's Wergild? It is told that when some of the Æsir, Odin and Loki and Hœnir, set out to explore the earth, they came to a river and followed it to a waterfall. Beside the waterfall was an otter, which had taken a salmon from the falls and was eating it, blinking its eyes as it ate. Then Loki picked up a stone and threw it at the otter, and hit it on the head. And Loki boasted of his catch, that he had got an otter and a salmon with one blow. They picked up the salmon and the otter and carried them along, and coming to the buildings of a farm, they went in. The farmer who lived there was called Hreidmarr; he was a man of great wealth, and very skilled in black magic. The Æsir asked him for a night's lodging, saying that they had enough food with them, and showed him their catch.

s-c46-2.s: But when Hreidmarr saw the otter, he at once called his sons, Fáfnir and Reginn, and told them that their brother Otr had been killed, and who had done it.

"Now father and sons went up to the Æsir, seized them, bound them, and told them about the otter, that he was Hreidmarr's son. The Æsir offered a ransom for their lives, as much wealth as Hreidmarr himself chose to name; and an agreement was made between them on those terms, and confirmed with oaths. Then the otter was skinned, and Hreidmarr, taking the otter-skin, told them to fill the skin with red gold and also to cover it completely; and that was to be the condition of the agreement between them.

s-c46-3.s: Then Odin sent Loki into Svartálfaheimr, and he came to the dwarf called Andvari, who was in the water as a fish. Loki caught him in his hands and demanded, as ransom for his life, all the gold he had in his rock; and when they came inside the rock, the dwarf brought out all the gold he had, and it was a very great treasure. Then the dwarf quickly slipped one little gold ring under his hand, but Loki saw it and ordered him to hand over the ring. The dwarf begged him not to take the ring from him, saying that with this ring he could multiply wealth for himself if he could keep it. Loki answered that he should not have one penny left, took the ring from him and went out; but the dwarf declared that the ring would be the ruin of everyone who came to own it. Loki replied that this suited him well enough, and that this condition would hold good provided that he himself brought it to the ears of those who would receive the ring and the curse.

s-c46-4.s: He went on his way and came to Hreidmarr's house, and showed the gold to Odin. When Odin saw the ring it seemed beautiful to him, and he took it out of the treasure, and paid the gold to Hreidmarr. Then Hreidmarr filled the otter-skin as full as he could, and stood it up when it was full. Next Odin went up to cover the skin with gold, and he told Hreidmarr to look and see whether the skin was now completely hidden. Hreidmarr looked at it closely, and saw one hair of the snout, and ordered that this be covered, or else their agreement would be at an end. Then Odin drew out the ring and covered the hair, saying that they were now free of their debt for the killing of the otter.

s-c46-5.s: But when Odin had taken his spear, and Loki his shoes, and they no longer had any need to be afraid, Loki declared that the curse Andvari had spoken would be fulfilled: that this ring and this gold would be the destruction of whoever received it; and so it later proved. Now it has been told why gold is called Otter's Wergild, or Forced Payment of the Æsir, or Metal of Strife.

s-c47-1.s: "What more is there to say about the gold? Hreidmarr took the gold as wergild for his son, but Fáfnir and Reginn claimed a share of their brother's blood-money for themselves. Hreidmarr would not grant them one penny of the gold. This was the wicked plan of those brothers: they killed their father for the gold.

s-c47-2.s: Then Reginn demanded that Fáfnir share the gold with him, half and half. Fáfnir answered that there was little chance of his sharing it with his brother, seeing that he had killed his father for it; and he told Reginn to go away, or else he would fare just as Hreidmarr had. Fáfnir had taken the helmet which had been Hreidmarr's and set it on his head (this helmet was called the Helmet of Terror, and all living creatures that see it are afraid of it), and the sword called Hrotti. Reginn had the sword called Refill. So he fled, and Fáfnir went up to Gnita Heath, made himself a lair, turned himself into a serpent and lay down on the gold.
"Then Reginn went to King Hjálprekr at Thjód, and became his smith there; and he took as his foster-son Sigurdr, son of Sigmundr, Völsungr's son, and of Hjördís, daughter of Eylimi.

s-c47-3.s: Sigurdr was the most illustrious of all Host-Kings in lineage, in prowess and in mind. Reginn told him where Fáfnir lay on the gold, and urged him to go after the gold.

s-c47-4.s: Then Reginn made the sword Gramr, which was so sharp that Sigurdr, lowering it into running water, cut in two a tuft of wool that drifted downstream onto the sword's edge. Next Sigurdr split Reginn's anvil down to the block with the sword.

s-c47-5.s: After that Sigurdr and Reginn went to Gnita Heath, and there Sigurdr dug a pit in Fáfnir's path and lay in ambush in it. When Fáfnir glided towards the water and came over the pit, Sigurdr at once thrust his sword through him, and that was his death.

"Then Reginn came up, saying that Sigurdr had killed his brother, and demanded as a condition of settlement that he take Fáfnir's heart and roast it over the fire; and Reginn lay down and drank Fáfnir's blood, and settled himself to sleep.

s-c47-6.s: But when Sigurdr was roasting the heart, and thought it must be fully roasted, he touched it with his finger to see how hard it was; and the juice ran out of the heart onto his finger, so that he was burned and put his finger in his mouth. As soon as the heart's blood touched his tongue, he at once knew the speech of birds, and he understood what the nuthatches sitting in the trees were saying. Then one said:

l: wise he would seem to me,
he means to betray the youth

s-c47-9.s: Then Sigurdr went over to Reginn and killed him, and from there to his horse, which was called Grani, and rode until he came to Fáfnir's lair. He took up the gold, packed it in his saddlebags, laid it on Grani's back, mounted himself, and rode on his way.

s-c47-10.s: Now the story has been told of why gold is called Lair or Abode of Fáfnir, or Metal of Gnita Heath, or Grani's Burden.

s-c48-1.s: "Then Sigurdr rode on until he found a house on the mountain, and in it a woman lay sleeping in helmet and mail-coat. He drew his sword and cut the mail-coat off her. Then she woke and gave her name as Hildr: she is called Brynhildr, and was a Valkyrie.

s-c48-2.s: Sigurdr rode away and came to a king called Gjúki, whose wife was Grímhildr. Their children were Gunnarr, Högni, Gudrún and Gudný; Gotthormr was Gjúki's stepson. Sigurdr stayed there a long time, and then he married Gudrún, the daughter of Gjúki, and Gunnarr and Högni swore oaths of blood brotherhood with Sigurdr.

s-c48-3.s: After that Sigurdr and the sons of Gjúki went to Atli, Budli's son, to ask for the hand of his sister Brynhildr in marriage to Gunnarr. Brynhildr lived on Hinda-Fell, and around her hall there was a flaring fire; and she had made a solemn vow to take no man but the one who dared to ride through the flaring fire.

"Then Sigurdr and the sons of Gjúki (who were also called Niflungs) rode up onto the mountain, and Gunnarr was to have ridden through the flaring fire. But he had the horse called Goti, and that horse did not dare to leap into the fire.

s-c48-4.s: So Sigurdr and Gunnarr exchanged shapes, and names as well, for Grani would carry no man but Sigurdr. Then Sigurdr leapt onto Grani and rode through the flaring fire. That evening he was married to Brynhildr. But when they went to bed, he drew the sword Gramr from its sheath and laid it between them. In the morning, when he got up and dressed, he gave Brynhildr as a linen-fee the same gold ring that Loki had taken from Andvari, and took another ring from her hand as a keepsake. Then Sigurdr mounted his horse and rode to his companions, and he and Gunnarr changed shapes again and went home to Gjúki with Brynhildr. Sigurdr and Gudrún had two children, Sigmundr and Svanhildr.

s-c49-1.s: "It happened one day that Brynhildr and Gudrún went to the water to wash their hair. When they came to the river, Brynhildr waded out from the bank well into the river, saying that she would not let the water that ran out of Gudrún's hair touch her head, since she herself had the braver husband.

s-c49-2.s: Then Gudrún went into the river after her and said that it was her right to wash her hair higher upstream, because she had as her husband a man whom neither Gunnarr nor anyone else in the world could match in courage, since he had killed Fáfnir and Reginn and inherited the wealth of both.

s-c49-3.s: And Brynhildr answered: 'It was worth more that Gunnarr rode through the flaring fire and Sigurdr did not dare.'

s-c49-4.s: Then Gudrún laughed and said: 'Do you think that Gunnarr rode through the flaring fire? I think that the man who went into the bridal bed with you was the same one who gave me this gold ring. And the gold ring that you wear on your hand, and received as a linen-fee, is called Andvaranautr, and I do not believe that it was Gunnarr who won that ring on Gnita Heath.'

s-c49-5.s: Then Brynhildr was silent, and went home.

"After that she urged Gunnarr and Högni to kill Sigurdr; but because they were Sigurdr's sworn blood-brothers, they stirred up their brother Gotthormr to kill him. He thrust his sword through Sigurdr as he slept; but when Sigurdr felt the wound, he hurled his sword Gramr after Gotthormr, so that it cut the man in two at the waist. There Sigurdr fell, and Sigmundr, his three-year-old son, whom they killed. Then Brynhildr stabbed herself with a sword, and she was burned with Sigurdr; but Gunnarr and Högni took Fáfnir's heritage and Andvaranautr, and ruled the lands from then on.

s-c50-1.s: "King Atli, Budli's son and the brother of Brynhildr, then married Gudrún, who had been Sigurdr's wife, and they had children. King Atli invited Gunnarr and Högni to visit him, and they came at his invitation. But before they left their own land they hid the gold, Fáfnir's heritage, in the Rhine, and that gold has never been found since. Now King Atli had an army ready, and fought with Gunnarr and Högni, and they were taken prisoner. King Atli ordered the heart to be cut out of Högni while he was alive, and that was his end. Gunnarr he had thrown into a pit of serpents. But a harp was brought secretly to Gunnarr, and he played it with his toes, since his hands were bound. He played the harp so that all the serpents fell asleep, except for one adder, which glided over to him and gnawed into the cartilage of his breastbone so deeply that her head sank into the wound, and she clung to his liver until he died. Gunnarr and Högni were called Niflungs and Gjúkungs, and for that reason gold is called Treasure, or Heritage, of the Niflungs.

s-c50-2.s: ["A little while later Gudrún killed her two sons and had flagons made from their skulls, set with gold and silver. Then the funeral feast was held for the Niflungs, and at this feast Gudrún had mead poured into the flagons for King Atli, and the mead was mixed with the blood of the boys. She also had their hearts roasted and set before the king for him to eat. And when he had eaten, she herself told him what she had done, with many bitter words. There was no shortage of strong drink there, so that most of the company had fallen asleep where they sat. That night she went to the king while he slept, and Högni's son with her; they struck the king, and that was his death. Then they set fire to the hall and burned the people who were inside.

s-c50-3.s: After that she went to the shore and leapt into the sea, meaning to put an end to herself; but the waves tossed her across the fjord, and she was carried to King Jónakr's land. When he saw her, he took her in and married her, and they had three sons, called Sörli, Hamdir and Erpr. They all had hair as black as a raven, like Gunnarr and Högni and the other Niflungs.

s-c50-4.s: There Svanhildr, the daughter of young Sigurdr, was brought up, and she was the most beautiful of all women. King Jörmunrekkr the Mighty heard of her beauty, and sent his son Randvér to woo her and bring her to be his wife. When Randvér came to Jónakr's court, Svanhildr was given into his hands, and he was to have brought her to King Jörmunrekkr. But Earl Bikki said that it would be better for Randvér to marry Svanhildr, since he and she were both young, whereas Jörmunrekkr was old. This advice pleased the young people well. Then Bikki reported the matter to the king. At once King Jörmunrekkr ordered his son to be seized and led to the gallows. Then Randvér took his hawk, plucked off its feathers and asked for it to be sent like that to his father; after which he was hanged. But when King Jörmunrekkr saw the hawk, it suddenly came home to him that just as the hawk was featherless and unable to fly, so his kingdom was stripped of its strength, since he was old and childless. Then King Jörmunrekkr, riding out of the wood where he had been hunting, saw Svanhildr as she sat washing her hair. They rode at her and trampled her to death under their horses' hooves.

s-c50-5.s: "But when Gudrún heard of this, she urged her sons to take vengeance for Svanhildr. When they were getting ready for their journey, she gave them mail-coats and helmets so strong that iron could not bite into them. She gave them these instructions: that when they came to King Jörmunrekkr, they should go up to him by night as he slept:
Sörli and Hamdir were to cut off his hands and feet, and Erpr his head.

s-c50-6.s: But when they were on their way, they asked Erpr what help they could expect from him if they met King Jörmunrekkr. He answered that he would give them the kind of help that the hand gives the foot. They said that the help the foot got from the hand was nothing at all. They were so angry with their mother for sending them away with harsh words, and so eager to do what would hurt her most, that they killed Erpr, because she loved him most of all.

s-c50-7.s: A little later, as Sörli was walking, one of his feet slipped, and he steadied himself with his hand; and he said: 'Now the hand does help the foot; it would be better now if Erpr were alive.'

s-c50-8.s: Now when they came to King Jörmunrekkr by night, where he was sleeping, and cut off his hands and feet, he woke and called to his men and told them to get up.

s-c50-9.s: And then Hamdir said: 'The head would be off by now, if Erpr were alive.'

s-c50-10.s: Then the retainers got up and attacked them, but could not overcome them with weapons; and Jörmunrekkr called out to them to beat them with stones, and it was done. There Sörli and Hamdir fell, and now the whole house and offspring of Gjúki were dead.

s-c51-1.s: A daughter called Áslaug survived young Sigurdr; she was brought up with Heimir in Hlymdalir, and great families are descended from her. It is said that Sigmundr, Völsungr's son, was so strong that he could drink poison and come to no harm; and his son Sinfjötli and Sigurdr had such hard skin that no poison from outside could hurt them. That is why Bragi the poet has sung:

l: of the Völsung's Drink hung writhing
on the hook of the Foeman

s-c51-3.s: Most poets have made verses and various short tales from these stories. Bragi the Old wrote of the fall of Sörli and Hamdir in the song of praise that he composed about Ragnarr Lodbrók:

l: to an evil dream, among the princes
stained with blood, while swords were swirling:
a brawl broke out in the dwelling
fell on the floor where, severed,
were seen; into the fountain of the ale-cups
he fell headlong, mixed with gore:
on the Shield, Leaf of the Bushes
of Leifi's Land, it is painted.
the king's couch; and the brothers
ordered Gjúki's race to be struck
hard, who were eager to rob
and all to repay Jónakr's offspring
I see the slaughter of heroes
on the fair surface of the shield-rim;
with many tales marked on it.]"

s-c52-1.s: "Why is gold called Fródi's Meal? This is the story behind it. One of Odin's sons, called Skjöldr, from whom the Skjöldungs are descended, had his home and ruled in the kingdom that is now called Denmark, but was then known as Gotland. Skjöldr's son, who ruled the land after him, was called Fridleifr. Fridleifr's son was Fródi: he succeeded to the kingdom after his father, at the time when Augustus Caesar imposed peace on the whole world; at that time Christ was born. But because Fródi was the mightiest of all kings in the Northern lands, the peace was called by his name wherever the Danish tongue was spoken, and people call it the Peace of Fródi. No man harmed another, even if he met his father's killer or his brother's face to face, loose or bound. Nor was there any thief or robber then, so that a gold ring lay for a long time on Jalangr's Heath.

s-c52-2.s: King Fródi went to a feast in Sweden at the court of a king called Fjölnir, and there he bought two maidservants, Fenja and Menja; they were huge and strong.

s-c52-3.s: At that time two millstones were found in Denmark, so large that no one was strong enough to turn them. The nature of the mill was such that whatever the one who turned it asked for was ground out by the millstones. This mill was called Grótti. The man who gave King Fródi the mill was called Hengikjöptr.

s-c52-4.s: King Fródi had the maidservants led to the mill and told them to grind gold, and they did so. First they ground gold and peace and happiness for Fródi; then he would allow them rest or sleep no longer than the cuckoo was silent or a song could be sung. It is said that they sang the song called Gróttasöngr, and this is its beginning:

s-c52-6.s: And before they stopped singing, they ground out an army against Fródi, so that the sea-king called Mýsingr came there that same night and killed Fródi, taking a great deal of plunder. Then the Peace of Fródi was at an end. Mýsingr took Grótti with him, and Fenja and Menja as well, and told them to grind salt. At midnight they asked whether Mýsingr was not tired of salt. He told them to grind longer. They had ground only a little while when the ship sank; and ever since there has been a whirlpool in the sea where the water falls through the hole in the millstone. It was then that the sea became salt.

l: They were led to the flour-mill,
though he find his brother's killer
But he said not a word
than while one song is sung.'
from the bosom of the earth,
nor would she grind like this,
beneath the surface of the earth;
clay eats at the soles of our feet,
to the songs of us two
and set fire to the dwellings
I have heard that Fródi's handmaids
ground in the mill most gladly
the king lets peace be broken:
the fair cheeks of my axe-head,
is exalted with the good king's riches.
A great many men are glad

s-c54-1.s: "Why is gold called Kraki's Seed? In Denmark there was a king called Hrólfr Kraki, the most famous of all the kings of old for generosity, courage and graciousness. One example of his graciousness that is often told in stories is this. A poor little boy called Vöggr came into King Hrólfr's hall. At that time the king was young and slightly built. Vöggr came up before him and looked up at him, and the king said: 'What do you want to say, boy, since you are looking at me?' Vöggr answered: 'When I was at home, I heard it said that King Hrólfr at Hleidr was the greatest man in the northern lands; but now a little pole sits in the high seat, and he is called king.' Then the king answered: 'You have given me a name, boy, so that I shall be called Hrólfr the Pole (Kraki); and it is the custom for a gift to go with the giving of a name. Now I see that you have no gift to go with the name you have fastened on me, none that I would care to accept, so the one who has something to give shall give to the other.' And he took a gold ring from his hand and gave it to him. Then Vöggr said: 'May you be the most blessed of givers, above all kings! Now I swear an oath that I will kill the man who kills you.' Then the king said, laughing loudly: 'Vöggr is pleased with a small thing.'

"Another example is the story told of Hrólfr Kraki's courage. A king called Adils ruled over Uppsala; he was married to Yrsa, the mother of Hrólfr Kraki. He was at war with the king who ruled Norway, whose name was Áli, and the two met in battle on the ice of the lake called Vaeni. King Adils sent messengers to Hrólfr Kraki, his stepson, asking him to come to his aid, and promised pay to his whole army for as long as they were away; King Hrólfr himself was to have three precious gifts, whichever three he chose from all Sweden. {p. 171} King Hrólfr could not make the journey himself, because of the war he was fighting against the Saxons; but he sent Adils his twelve berserks. Bödvar-Bjarki was one of them, and Hjalti the Stout-Hearted, Hvítserkr the Stern, Vöttr, Véseti, and the brothers Svipdagr and Beigudr. In that battle King Áli fell, and most of his army with him; and King Adils took from the dead man the helmet Battle-Swine and his horse Raven.

s-c54-2.s: Then Hrólfr Kraki's berserks demanded their pay, three pounds of gold for each of them; and in addition they asked to take to Hrólfr Kraki the precious gifts they had chosen for him. These were the helmet Hildisvín and the mail-coat Finnsleif, neither of which iron could bite, and the gold ring called Svíagríss, which had belonged to Adils' forefathers. But the king refused them all these things, and did not even pay their wages. The berserks went away ill-pleased with their share, and told Hrólfr Kraki how things stood.

s-c54-3.s: "At once he set out for Uppsala; and when he had brought his ships into the river Fýri, he rode straight to Uppsala, and his twelve berserks with him, all without safe-conduct. Yrsa, his mother, welcomed him and took him to lodgings, but not to the king's hall. Fires were lit there in front of them, and they were given ale to drink. Then King Adils' men came in and heaped firewood onto the fire, and made it so great that the clothes were burnt off Hrólfr and his men. s-c61-1.s: "Weapons and armour should be periphrased in terms of battle, and with reference to Odin and the Valkyries and host-kings. One should call a helmet Cowl, or Hood; a mail-coat, Shirt, or Tunic; a shield, Tent; and a shield-wall is called Hall and Roof, Wall and Floor. Shields, periphrased in terms of warships, are called Sun, or Moon, or Leaf, or Sheen, or Fence, of the Ship; the shield is also called Ship of Ullr, or periphrased in terms of Hrungnir's feet, since he stood on his shield. s-c62-7.s: Then they began the famous battle called Hjadningavíg. They fought all that day, but in the evening the kings went to their ships. s-c66-9.s: It is also right to call a king King of Kings if he has tributary kings under him. s-c66-11.s: Next to these in the figures of poetry are the men called chiefs. They may be periphrased as one might a king or an earl, by calling them Dispensers of Gold, Wealth Munificent, Men of the Standards, and Captains of the Host, or Van-Leaders of the Array or of Battle. For every king of a nation who rules over many lands appoints tributary kings and earls to share authority with him, to administer the laws of the land and defend it from attack in those parts that lie far away from the king. And in those parts they are to be equal with the king himself in giving judgment and dealing out punishment. Now there are many districts in one land, and it is the practice of kings to appoint magistrates over as many districts as they choose to put into their hands. These magistrates are called chiefs or landed men in the Danish tongue, reeves in Saxony, and barons in England. They are also to be just judges and faithful warriors over the land entrusted to them to govern. If the king is not near, a standard is to be carried before them in battle; and then they are just as lawful war-captains as kings or earls.

"Next below them are the men called franklins: these are the freeholders who are of honourable family and have full rights. They may be periphrased by calling them Wealth-Givers, and Protectors, and Reconcilers of Men; leaders may have these titles too.

s-c78-3.s: ["It is autumn from the equinox until the time when the sun sets three and a half hours after noon; then winter lasts until the equinox; then it is spring until the moving-days; then summer until the equinox. s-c80-1.s: "There was a king called Hálfdan the Old, who was the most famous of all kings. He held a great sacrificial feast at midwinter, and sacrificed in order that he might live three hundred years in his kingdom. But this was the answer he received: he would live no longer than the full life of a man, but for three hundred years there would be no woman and no man in his line who was not of great repute. He was a great warrior, and went raiding far and wide in Austrvegrs; there he killed in single combat the king called Sigtryggr. Then he married the woman called Alvig the Wise, daughter of King Eymundr of Hólmgardr. They had eighteen sons, nine born at one birth. These were their names: the first, Thengill, who was called Manna-Thengill; the second, Ræsir; the third, Gramr; the fourth, Gylfi; the fifth, Hilmir; the sixth, Jöfurr; the seventh, Tyggi; the eighth, Skyli or Skúli; the ninth, Harri or Herra. These nine brothers became so famous for their raiding that, in all records since, their names have been used as titles of rank, like the name of King or that of Earl. They had no children, and all fell in battle. As Ottarr the Swarthy sang:

s-c80-19.s: "Hálfdan and his wife also had nine other sons. From the family of the Hildings came Haraldr the Red-Bearded, the mother's father of Hálfdan the Swarthy. Of the Niflung's house was Gjúki; of the house of the Ödlings, Kjárr; of the house of the Ylfings was Eiríkr the Wise in Speech.

s-c81-1.s: "Poets are called bards, and in poetry it is correct to call any man so, if one wishes. The men who served King Hálfr were called Champions, and from their name warriors are called champions; and it is correct to call all men so. In poetry men are also called Lofdar, as is written above. The men who served the king named Skati the Munificent were called Skatnar: from his name everyone who is munificent is called Skati. Those who followed Bragi the Old were called Bragnar. Those who assess the dealings of men are called assessors. Those who defend the land are called Fyrdar and Firar. Vikings and fleet-men make up a ship-army. Those who followed King Beimuni were called Beimar. Captains of companies are called Grooms, just as the man who brings home a bride is called. The Goths are named after the king who was called Goti, from whom Gotland is named. He was so called after Odin's name, derived from the name Gautr, for Gautland or Gotland was named after Odin's name, and Sweden from the name of Svidurr, which is also a title of Odin's. At that time all the mainland that he possessed was called Reid-Gotaland, and all the islands Ey-Gotaland: that is now called the Realm of Danes or of Swedes.

"Young men who are not householders are called Drengs while they are gaining wealth and glory. Seafaring Drengs are those who voyage from land to land; King's Drengs are those who serve rulers. Those who serve wealthy men or freeholders are Drengs too; and valiant and ambitious men are called Drengs.

s-c81-2.s: Warriors are also called Champions and Troops: these are soldiers. Freeholders are called Thanes and Yeomen; the men who go about reconciling people are called Day-Men. These are the men who are called Champions, Fighters, Men of War, Brave Men, Valiant Men, Hardy Men, Overpowerers, Heroes. Set against these are the following terms: Soft, Weak, Unleavened, Leavenless, Melting One, Sheath, Coward, Skulker, Weakling, Qualmish, Wretch, Scamp, Vile One, Dog, Lout, Feeble One, Paltry One, Imbecile, Bungler, Son of Wretchedness.

"An open-handed man is called Munificent, Illustrious, Towerer, Mighty Towerer, Towering Gold-Giver, Prince of Men, Wealthy One, Prosperous, Heaper-Up of Riches, Mighty Man, Chieftain. In contrast to these are those who are called Niggard, Miser, Calculator, Wretched One, Wealth-Hiding, Gift-Tardy One. A man wise in counsel is called Wielder of Counsel. A witless man is called Clown, Oaf, Gander, Dupe, Boor, Idiot, Dolt, Fool, Madman, Maniac, Moon-Struck. One who thinks a great deal of dress is called Gaudy, Dreng, Glittering One, Careful of Attire, Tricked-Out. A noisy fellow is called Shark-Skin, Braggart, Sheath-Cleaner, Fawner, Brawler, Good-for-Nothing, Worthless One.

s-c81-3.s: The common folk are called Country-folk or People. A slave is called Kept-Man, Serf, Labourer, Servant.

s-c82-1.s: "Each one singly is called a man; it is a pair if there are two; three are a hamlet; four are a group; a band is five men; if there are six, it is a squad; seven complete a crew; eight men make a panel; nine are 'good fellows'; ten are a gang; eleven form an embassy; it is a dozen if twelve go together; thirteen are a crowd; fourteen are an expedition; it is a gathering when fifteen meet; sixteen make a garrison; seventeen are a congregation; to the man who meets eighteen, they seem enemies enough. He who has nineteen men has a company; twenty men are a posse; thirty are a squadron; forty, a community; fifty are a shire; sixty are an assembly; seventy are a line; eighty are a people; one hundred is a host.

s-c83-1.s: "Besides these there are the terms that men put before the names of men: we call such terms epithets of possession, or true terms, or surnames. It is an epithet of possession when one names a thing by its true name and calls the man one wishes to periphrase Owner of that thing, or Father or Grandfather of what was named; Grandsire is a third epithet. A son, moreover, is also called Heir, Heritor, Bairn, Child and Boy, Inheritor. A blood-kinsman is called Brother, Twin, Full Brother, Blood-Kin; a relation is also called Nephew, Kinsman, Kin, Kith, Friend, Kin-Stave, Descendant, Family-Prop, Family-Stem, Kin-Branch, Family-Bough, Offshoot, Offspring, Head-Tree, Scion. Kinsmen by marriage are further called Sib-folk, Minglers of Blood. A friend is called Counsel-Mate, Counsel-Giver, Adviser, Secret-Sharer, Converser, Bench-Fellow, Favourite, Seat-Mate; bench-fellow also means Cabin-Mate. A foe is called Adversary, Shooter Against One, Hater, Attacker, Harmer, Slayer, Hard Presser, Pursuer, Overbearer.
"These terms we call epithets of possession; and it is the same if a man is known by his dwelling or his ship, when it has a name of its own, or by his estate, when a name of its own is given to it.
"This is what we call true terms: to call a man Wise Man, Man of Thought, Wise in Speech, Sage in Counsel, Wealth Munificent, Not Slack, Endower, Illustrious One; these are surnames.

s-c84-1.s: "These are simple terms for women in poetry: Wife and Bride and Matron are the women who are given to a man. Those who go about in pomp and fine clothes are called Dame and Lady. Those who are witty in speech are called Women of Wisdom. Those who are gentle are called Girls; those who carry themselves proudly are called Proud and Haughty Ones. She who is noble-minded is called Gentlewoman; she who is richest, Lady. She who is bashful, as young girls are, or those women who are modest, is called Lass. The woman whose husband has left the land is called Stay-at-Home.

The woman whose husband has been killed is called War-Widow: Widow is the term for her whose husband has died of sickness. Maid means, first, every woman, and then crones who are old. Then there are the terms for women that are insulting: one may find them in poems, though they are not written down. Women who have one husband in common are called Concubines. A son's wife is termed Daughter-in-law; the husband's mother is called Mother-in-law. A woman may also be called Mother, Grandmother, Great-Grandmother; a Mother is called Dam. Woman is further called Daughter, Bairn, and Child. She is also called Sister, Lady, and Maiden. Woman is also called Bed-Fellow, Speech-Mate, and Secret-Sharer of her husband; and that is an epithet of possession.

s-c85-1.s: "A man's head is termed thus: [this is how it should be periphrased: call it Toil or Burden of the Neck; Land of the Helmet, of the Hood, and of the Brain, of the Hair and Brows, of the Scalp, of Ears, Eyes, and Mouth; Sword of Heimdallr, and it is correct to use any term for sword that one wishes, and to periphrase it in terms of any one of the names of Heimdallr] the Head, in simple terms, is called Skull, Brain, Temple, Crown. The eyes are termed Vision or Glance, and Regard, Swift-Appraising; [they may be periphrased by calling them Sun or Moon, Shields and Glass or Jewels or Stones of the Eyelids, of the Brows, the Lashes, or the Forehead]. The ears are called Listeners or Hearing; [one should periphrase them by calling them Land, or any earth-name, or Mouth, or Canal, or Vision, or Eyes of Hearing, if the metaphors employed are newly coined. The mouth one should periphrase by calling it Land or House of the Tongue or of the Teeth, of Words or of the Palate, of the Lips, or the like; and if the metaphors used are not traditional, then men may call the mouth Ship, and the lips the Planks, and the tongue Oar or Tiller of the Ship. The teeth are sometimes called Gravel or Rocks of Words, of the Mouth, or of the Tongue. The tongue is often called Sword of Speech or of the Mouth]. The hair that grows on the lips is called Beard, Moustache, or Whiskers. Hair is called Nap; the hair of women is called Tresses. Hair is termed Locks. [One may periphrase hair by calling it Forest, or by some tree-name; one may periphrase it in terms of the skull or brain or head; and the beard in terms of chin or cheeks or throat.]

s-c86-1.s: The heart is called grain-sheaf; [one should periphrase it by calling it Grain or Stone or Apple or Nut or Ball, or the like, in terms of the breast or of feeling. It may also be called House or Earth or Mount of Feeling. One should periphrase the breast by calling it House or Enclosure or Ship of the Heart, of Breath, or of the Liver; Land of Energy, of Feeling, and of Memory]. Feeling is affection and emotion, love, passion, desire, love-longing. [Passion should be periphrased by calling it Wind of Troll Women; it is also correct to name whichever one of them one wishes, and to name giants, periphrasing giantesses as Woman or Mother or Daughter of the Giants.] Feeling is also called mood, liking, eagerness, courage, activity, memory, understanding, temper, humour, good faith. It is also wrath, enmity, mischievousness, grimness, balefulness, grief, sorrow, ill-will, spite, falseness, faithlessness, fickleness, light-mindedness, baseness, hasty temper, violence.

s-c87-1.s: "The hand and forearm may be called hand, arm, paw, palm. Parts of the arm are called elbow, upper arm, wolf's joint, finger, grip, wrist, nail, fingertip, hand-edge, quick. [One may call the hand Earth of Weapons or of Defensive Armour; and together with shoulder and arm, the hollow of the hand and the wrist, it may be called Earth of Gold Rings, of the Falcon and the Hawk, and of all the names for these; and in newly coined metaphors, Leg of the Shoulder-joint, and Force of the Bow. The legs may be called Tree of the Soles, of the Insteps, of the Ankles, or the like; Running Shaft of the Road or of the Way or the Pace; one may call the leg Tree or Post of all these. The legs are periphrased in metaphors of snowshoes, shoes, and breeches.] The parts of the legs are called thigh, knee, calf, lower leg, upper leg, instep, arch, sole, toe; [one may periphrase the leg in terms of all these, calling it their Tree, Mast, and Yard; and in metaphors of them all].

s-c88-1.s: "Speech is called words, language, eloquence, talk, tale, gibing, controversy, song, spell, recital, idle talk, babbling, din, chatter, squalling, merry noise, wrangling, mocking, quarrelling, drivel, boasting, tittle-tattle, nonsense, idiom, vanity, gabbling. It is also termed voice, sound, resonance, articulation, wailing, shriek, dash, crash, alarm, roaring, creaking, swoop, swooping, outburst.
"Understanding is called wisdom, counsel, discernment, memory, speculation, intelligence, arithmetic, far sight, craft, word-wit, pre-eminence. It is called subtlety, wiliness, falsehood, fickleness.

s-c89-1.s: "Expression is of two kinds: what is called voice, and what is called manners; manners is also temper. Reiði also has a double meaning: reiði is a man's ill humour, and reiði is also the rigging of a ship or the harness of a horse. Fár also has a double meaning: fár means wrath, and far means a ship.

"Men have made frequent use of ambiguous expressions such as these, and this practice is called punning. [Lith is the part of a man where bones meet; lið is a word for ship; lið means people; when a man gives another help, his aid is lið; líð means ale. Hlið means the gate in an enclosure; hliðr is what men call an ox, and hlíð means a slope. One may use these distinct meanings in poetry so as to make a pun that is hard to interpret, provided one employs other distinctions than those indicated by the preceding half-lines. These cases are there, and many others, in which various things have the same name in common.]"
